title: Core NLP Tasks
summary: The standard NLP task landscape and the go-to approach for each — the "how would you build X" interview questions.

slides.subTitle: Sentiment, topic — pipeline and metrics
slides.markdown: Text classification assigns one (or more) labels to a whole piece of text — sentiment (positive/negative/neutral), topic (sports/politics/tech), or intent (billing/support/sales). The standard modern pipeline: tokenize, run through a fine-tuned encoder model (or a classical TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline for a quick first pass), take the pooled representation, and output class probabilities via softmax. Evaluate with **accuracy** only when classes are balanced; otherwise **precision/recall/F1 per class** and a **confusion matrix**, since a model can hit 95% accuracy on a 95%-negative dataset by always predicting negative. Multi-label variants (a support ticket can be both "billing" and "urgent") use independent sigmoid outputs per label instead of one softmax.

slides.subTitle: Framed as sequence labeling
slides.markdown: NER identifies spans of text referring to entities (person, organization, location, date) and labels each. It's framed as **sequence labeling**: every token gets a tag, typically in **BIO format** — `B-PER` (beginning of a person entity), `I-PER` (inside/continuation), `O` (outside any entity). "Barack Obama visited Paris" tags as `B-PER I-PER O O B-LOC`. This per-token framing is what lets a single model handle entities of arbitrary length and multiple entities in one sentence, and it's why NER fine-tuning heads apply a classifier at every token position rather than pooling to one vector like classification does.

slides.subTitle: The seq2seq framing and the BLEU score
slides.markdown: Translation is the archetypal **sequence-to-sequence** task: input and output are different-length sequences in different vocabularies, which is exactly what encoder-decoder Transformers were originally built for — see [Attention & Transformer Architecture](attention-transformer-architecture). Evaluation uses **BLEU**, which measures n-gram overlap between the model's output and one or more human reference translations, with a brevity penalty to stop the model gaming the score with short outputs. BLEU's real weakness: it rewards surface-level n-gram matches, so a fluent, semantically correct translation using different phrasing than the reference can score lower than a clunky one that happens to match more n-grams — which is why human evaluation and newer learned metrics increasingly supplement BLEU in practice.

slides.subTitle: Extractive vs generative QA
slides.markdown: **Extractive QA** finds the answer as a literal span within a given passage — the model predicts start and end token positions, and the answer is guaranteed to be text that actually appears in the source (this is what SQuAD-style benchmarks and BERT's QA head do). **Generative QA** produces a free-form answer, potentially synthesizing or paraphrasing across multiple sources, or answering from parametric knowledge with no passage at all — this is what LLMs do by default. The trade-off: extractive QA can't answer questions that require combining information from two sentences or reasoning beyond the literal text, but it also can't hallucinate, since every answer is a verifiable substring; generative QA is more flexible but must be checked for fabricated claims.

slides.subTitle: Extractive vs abstractive
slides.markdown: **Extractive summarization** selects and stitches together existing sentences from the source verbatim — simpler, always factually grounded in the source, but often reads disjointedly. **Abstractive summarization** generates new sentences that paraphrase and condense, closer to how a human would summarize — more fluent and coherent, but capable of introducing claims not actually supported by the source (the same hallucination risk as generative QA). Modern production summarizers are almost always abstractive (LLM-based), with extractive methods now mostly used as a cheap first-pass filter or as a fallback when factual grounding must be guaranteed.

slides.sectionTitle: Three ways to solve the same task
slides.subTitle: Rule-based vs fine-tuned transformer vs LLM-prompted
slides.markdown:
| | Rule-based / classical ML | Fine-tuned transformer | LLM-prompted |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data needed | Little to none (hand rules) or small labeled set | Thousands of labeled examples | Zero to a handful of examples (few-shot) |
| Setup speed | Fast to write, slow to maintain | Slower (needs training pipeline) | Fastest to prototype |
| Accuracy ceiling | Lower, brittle to phrasing | High, if enough labeled data | High, but less predictable/controllable |
| Cost per request | Very low | Low | Higher (API cost, latency) |

How to decide: rule-based for a narrow, stable pattern (email regex extraction); fine-tuned transformer when you have labeled data and need cheap, high-volume, predictable inference; LLM-prompted when you have little labeled data, the task shifts often, or you need to move fast and can absorb the per-request cost.
